extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of municipal government, municipal reformers, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for organizing, supervising, and reforming municipal functions (budgeting, police, courts, health, tenement, fire, streets, lighting, and transportation). Focused on what effective municipal administration should do and how departments should be structured and operated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure of tentative budget and hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal features of the tentative budget should be made public and further hearings granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing leading items of the tentative budget, also state which citizen demands were rejected; use publication and hearings to increase public control and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricting use of appropriated funds without authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A resolution should accompany every budget that 'moneys therein appropriated may not be used for other purposes without authority from the appropriating body and without due notice to the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents public officers from diverting funds to purposes other than indicated in the appropriation; accompanies broader public control over disbursement as well as budget-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of payrolls to prevent early expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts voted for each payroll should be divided so that disbursements for any one month do not exceed one-twelfth of the total annual appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule recommended to prevent department heads from spending allowances early in the fiscal year and becoming 'bankrupt' later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern business methods, inspection and audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments should have 'modern business methods of describing work done when done, and money spent when spent, plus methods of inspection and of audit' from the first day of the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessary to make possible and ensure execution of budgetary controls and to verify compliance and truthful accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public control over disbursement as well as budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Public control must extend beyond making the budget to the disbursement of funds to prevent misuse by public officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates procedural and institutional checks (resolutions, audits, inspections) to ensure appropriated funds are used for intended purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: State versus local control of police
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate between vesting police control in state authorities vs local authorities: state control aims to protect 'public decency and order' from corrupt local sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York's 1857 metropolitan police under a state commission; suggestion of state inspection and state detective forces to coordinate and check local police.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatton's plan for coordinating state and local police
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific recommendations: (1) police commissioner in each city appointed by mayor, term during good behavior, removable by mayor after public statement of charges; (2) mayors/police commissioners/sheriffs removable by governor after public statement for delinquency or corruption; (3) state inspection of local police; (4) a small but efficient state detective force under the governor; (5) centralization of state inspection and detective work in a state bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offered as a scheme to coordinate state and local control and to guard against local corrupt influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of board system for police supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Board systems that spread police supervision over multiple members were found to encourage division of spoils and to diffuse responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience led many large cities to abandon boards and concentrate supervision in a single officer to fix responsibility and improve accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized police commissioner with clear powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrate authority and responsibility in a single police commissioner (example: New York commissioner appointed by mayor for five years, removable by mayor, with power to appoint deputy commissioners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralization makes it easier for citizens to apply pressure via the mayor when enforcement is lax; must balance central power with mechanisms to ensure permanence/authority where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure/permanence of police leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of permanence in police commissioners undermines their command because subordinate officers (permanent, politically influenced) look past temporary chiefs to more permanent influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability or appropriate tenure provisions can help ensure a commissioner's orders are carried out and reduce patronage influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military/uniformed organization and graded hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Police forces are organized on a military principle with graded authorities from patrolman up to chief, precincts with patrolmen, sergeants/roundsmen, captains, inspectors, and central chiefs and deputies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure facilitates discipline, central control, and inspection districts to watch conduct of subordinates; uniforming was historically controversial but later accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized police divisions and detective bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Large cities should have special divisions (bicycle squad, mounted squad, river & harbor squads) and a corps of detectives connected with a central bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization improves capability to handle diverse policing tasks and facilitates central supervision under the commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and mechanisms of police corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Police corruption arises from opportunities for discrimination/persecution, monetary payoffs from saloons/gamblers/vice establishments, and political pressures via campaign contributions and party machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both monetary and political inducements; corruption is aided by laws penalizing actions not seen as harmful by the majority, creating revenue opportunities for 'immunity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service examinations to prevent spoils in patrol selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide civil service examinations for patrolmen to prevent the spoils system from entering police rank-and-file selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited adoption in New York, Milwaukee and other large cities as protection against patronage and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and tenure of police magistrates and judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges who try offenders should be 'in close and sympathetic touch with the social and economic conditions' of defendants; election of magistrates can bring them close to district life but can also subject them to political boss control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the risk of boss influence, several cities abandoned elective systems in favor of appointment with long terms (example: New York city magistrates appointed by mayor for ten years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of children's (juvenile) courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate juvenile offenders from hardened adult lawbreakers and treat them as delinquents needing care and supervision rather than as criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: avoid commitment of first offenders to institutions; release on probation unless home influences are pernicious; create probation officers to visit homes and monitor reform; success depends on tact, humanity, and wisdom of probation officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation and home-environment investigation for juveniles
rubrics_metrics.description: Probation officers should investigate home conditions and supervise compliance with court instructions; parental failure to correct may lead to commitment and orders to pay maintenance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juvenile courts aim to rescue children and view each as a 'prospective citizen'; statistical example: of 11,494 children arraigned in 1909 only 1,792 committed to institutions in one court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded scope of public health officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Health officers should control abatement of nuisances, enforcement against adulterated foods, milk inspection, collection of vital statistics, and suppression of infectious diseases, and should regard prevention as central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern health departments establish school clinics, milk stations, fight tenement overcrowding and unsanitary factory conditions; 'public health is purchasable' and communities can determine death rates within natural limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenement house and building department standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments charged with maintaining standards in construction regarding light, air, sanitary conditions, and fire protection, including inspection and enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model housing laws typically set percentage of lot area tenement may occupy, maximum heights, water supply for each apartment, room sizes and window space, owner duties to keep courts/halls/yards clean, and provide inspection officers to report violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire department professionalization and prevention focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire departments should evolve from voluntary to regular professional forces with improved organization, technical equipment, civil service requirements, pensions, and an emphasis on prevention as a vital municipal function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many large cities now have fire prevention bureaus to study causes and methods of avoiding fires; prevention is as important as response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws and inspection to control inflammable materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Enact laws and ordinances controlling inflammable materials and place enforcement in prevention bureaus' inspection forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection and enforcement aim to reduce losses caused by defective construction and inadequate supervision of private buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of insurance practices that encourage arson
rubrics_metrics.description: Loose insurance practices (overinsuring goods, allowing huge policies on small dwellings) have been discovered to encourage merchants to set fires to recoup losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for study and criticism of insurance laxness as a contributor to yearly fire losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-paved streets as municipal economy and aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-paved street is an economy for private vehicle owners and an aesthetic improvement; many cities have moved from gravel and cobblestone to granite, asphalt, and wooden blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage invention and adoption of new paving materials and better methods of laying and preserving pavements; public sentiment should protest slovenly streets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved street-cleaning organization and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities should develop thorough methods of street cleaning rather than relying on unskilled casual day labor; establish separate street-cleaning departments with regulation of sidewalks and refuse disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York's department (1881) and Colonel Waring's reforms—military discipline, uniforms, organization—dignified work and improved cooperation across large forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waste separation and treatment plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Require citizens to separate decaying vegetable matter from ashes and waste papers and establish reduction/treatment plants for collected wastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatment plants can reduce disposal costs and may generate revenue from sale of byproducts (example: Cleveland 1907 financials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Street lighting systems and ownership models
rubrics_metrics.description: Street lighting moved from gas to electric; municipalities previously relied on private corporations for gas lighting; municipal ownership of electric plants is more common and often more successful than municipal gas ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics: by 1899 electric plants outnumbered gas plants; by 1903 a minority of larger cities owned gas works, but more owned electric plants (examples: Chicago, Detroit owned electric plants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal responsibility for passenger transportation infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities must address transporting large numbers of passengers—transitioning from horse-cars to cable systems, electric roads, elevated railways, and subways as population grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York's elevated lines (1870) and subway (1904); the shift to underground/express/local/elevated combinations in dense urban corridors; growth of track mileage demonstrates need for municipal planning and large-scale infrastructure.
